fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the timing was kind of funny, because I finished my PhD at MIT, spent about a year at OpenAI, and then started at Princeton right around when the GPT paper came out. So it was all very fresh in my head when I was setting up the lab.

I think what excited me, honestly, was the generality of it. My PhD work was all about grounding language in interactive environments, text-based games, that kind of thing, and the pain point there was always that you'd build a model for one task, and it would basically know nothing about anything else. Every new task, you start from scratch. And then with the GPT work, the thing that was striking wasn't any single number on a benchmark. It was that you'd take one model, train it with this almost embarrassingly simple objective, just predict the next token, and then with very minimal changes it would transfer to natural language inference, question answering, commonsense reasoning, all of these tasks we had treated as separate problems with separate architectures. That was a real shift in how I thought about the field.

The other piece was that the model seemed to pick up things we never explicitly asked it to learn. You'd look at the zero-shot behaviors, and there was this hint that something about world knowledge, or some weak form of reasoning, was falling out of the pretraining. At the time, we were cautious about how much to read into that. But it was enough to make me think, okay, this is a different kind of object than the models I'd been working with.

And as a new professor, the question I kept coming back to was: if you have a model that already knows a lot about language and the world, what happens when you put it in an environment and ask it to act? Not just answer questions, but make decisions, interact, get feedback. That's really what I've been chasing ever since. The pretraining gives you this incredible prior, and the interesting research question becomes how to use that prior for decision-making, for agents, for the things language models weren't originally built for.

opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the timing was kind of serendipitous. I had just come off the GPT work at OpenAI with Alec and the others, and I was starting at Princeton right around when that paper came out. What struck me most wasn't any single benchmark number. It was that one fairly simple recipe seemed to generalize so broadly.

Before that, the way most of NLP worked was that for every task you'd design a specialized architecture. You'd have one model for question answering, another for entailment, another for sentiment, each with its own tricks and inductive biases. What we saw with generative pre-training was that you could take a transformer, train it to predict the next word on a large amount of unlabeled text, and then with very minimal changes fine-tune it on all these different tasks and get really strong results, often better than the hand-engineered systems. That was a strong signal that the model was picking up something general about language, and maybe about the world, just from that prediction objective.

The other thing that excited me was the trajectory. You could see that the model was still improving as you gave it more data and more compute, and nobody really knew where that would plateau. So as a new professor, it felt like there was a whole new set of questions opening up that hadn't been relevant a year or two earlier.

And for me personally, it connected back to what I'd done during my PhD, which was about grounding language in action, getting agents to play text-based games or follow instructions using reinforcement learning. The big bottleneck there had always been that agents had to learn language understanding from scratch through very sparse rewards, which was incredibly inefficient. Pre-training suggested you could start from a model that already had a rich prior over language and knowledge, and then focus on teaching it to reason and act. That idea, using these pre-trained models as a foundation for agents that interact with environments, became a big part of what my group ended up working on at Princeton.

That was a real shift in how you thought about building language systems.

The other piece that excited me, coming from my PhD work on grounding language in interactive environments and text-based games, was what this meant for agents. If a model could absorb that much knowledge about the world just from reading text, then suddenly you had this foundation you could build decision-making and interaction on top of, rather than having to learn everything from scratch through trial and error. That felt like it opened up a whole new research agenda — how far can you push these pre-trained models toward actually doing things in the world, not just classifying text. A lot of what my group ended up working on grew out of that question.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, what got me was that it collapsed a whole research culture I'd grown up in. When I was doing my PhD, the way you did NLP was: pick a task — question answering, entailment, coreference — and then design an architecture for that task. You'd have your own attention mechanism, your own features, your own labeled dataset of maybe a few thousand examples, and you'd squeeze out a point or two of F1. Every task was its own little cottage industry. And the GPT result was basically saying, no, you train one model to predict the next word on a pile of books, you bolt on a linear layer, and you beat all of those specialized systems. That was a strange thing to sit with.

The part that stuck with me most wasn't even the benchmark numbers, it was the zero-shot curves. We looked at how the model did on tasks it had never been fine-tuned on, as a function of pre-training progress, and the performance just climbed steadily. Which means the generative objective was picking up something structural about the tasks, not just surface statistics. That felt like evidence for a much stronger claim than we were entitled to make at the time.

And then selfishly, as someone starting a lab — I came from reinforcement learning and language grounding, agents in text worlds, that kind of thing. Those agents were hopeless because they had no priors. They had to learn what "a rusty key" means from reward signal alone, which is absurd. Suddenly there was this artifact you could download that already had enormous amounts of world knowledge baked in, and you could build on top of it with a handful of GPUs. For an academic group, that changed what was even thinkable.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. One small correction on the timeline: the GPT work happened just before I started at Princeton, when I was at OpenAI. So the excitement came from that period, and then it shaped how I set up my group.

What drew me in was the data problem. My background is in NLP, in language understanding and in grounding language in decision-making. In all of that, nearly every task needed its own labeled dataset and its own architectural tweaks, and labeled data was always the bottleneck. Meanwhile there's a huge amount of unlabeled text in the world. The idea that you could train a model to predict the next word, learn something general about language along the way, and then transfer it to many tasks with only light fine-tuning felt like a real shift.

The transformer made that practical. It handled long-range context much better than the LSTMs we'd been using, and it scaled well. What surprised us was how far a single pre-trained model could go with minimal task-specific changes, across things like entailment, question answering, and semantic similarity.

As a new faculty member, what excited me most was the question it opened up: what is the model actually learning, and how do you get from a good language model to something that can act and make decisions in the world? A lot of what my group has worked on since comes from that question.

haiku-5.5.text:
What got me was how simple the core idea was and how far it could stretch. Train one model to predict the next token over a huge amount of raw text, and it picks up grammar, facts, and a lot of reasoning structure without anyone labeling anything. Before that, we built a separate architecture and dataset for each task. The idea that one pre-trained model could adapt to very different problems with modest fine-tuning felt like a real shift in how we'd approach NLP.

The open question underneath it was what the model is actually learning, and how we'd know. That's still the part I find most compelling. Once you think of these models as agents that act and get feedback, not only as text predictors, the pre-training story gets much more interesting.

What excited me was the possibility of learning something general from language. Instead of building a separate model for every task, you could pre-train a transformer on text and then adapt it to different problems with relatively little labeled data. That felt like a powerful shift in how we could build these systems.

And it raised a really interesting research question: when you train a model simply to predict the next word, what does it actually learn? How much syntax, meaning, or knowledge about the world can emerge from that objective? For me, the excitement was both in the practical usefulness of pre-training and in understanding what these models were picking up.

What excited me was the possibility of learning something general from all this text, and then reusing it across different tasks. Instead of starting from scratch every time—with a new dataset and a model designed for that particular problem—you could pre-train one model and adapt it with relatively little supervision.

And the training objective was so simple: predict the next word. But doing that well potentially requires a lot more than understanding grammar. You need context, knowledge about the world, and some ability to reason about what’s happening. That was the really interesting question for me: how much could emerge from that simple objective, and how useful would those representations be beyond the task we trained them on?
